title: Kouign-amann
subtitle: Breton caramelised butter cake from laminated bread dough
excerpt: Kouign-amann is a Breton cake made by folding butter and sugar into a yeasted bread dough, then baking at high heat until the sugar caramelises into a brittle, glassy crust. You get a cake that is part flaky pastry, part pull-apart bread, and part toffee slab. Watch the colour: once the caramel in the tin goes past deep amber, it is on its way to burnt.
sourceNotes: Kouign-amann (pronounced KWEEN ah-MAHN) was created in 1860 in Douarnenez, Brittany, by baker Yves-Rene Scordia. The name means butter cake in Breton. The recipe has been widely documented in French regional baking literature and is a standard example of laminated yeasted dough.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten warm from the oven or within 2 hours. The caramel crust softens as the cake cools. It can be refreshed for 5 minutes in a 180 degrees Celsius oven the next day.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. The caramel will bubble and may smoke at the end of baking; this is normal.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of folding a block of cold butter into a dough in repeated turns to create distinct alternating layers. In kouign-amann, sugar is folded in alongside the butter. During baking the sugar caramelises between the layers and the butter creates a flaky, slightly bready structure. Unlike croissant lamination, the process is rougher and faster: perfect even layers are not the goal.

The chemical process by which sugar molecules break down under heat to produce hundreds of new flavour compounds with bitter, nutty, and complex sweet notes. Caramelisation begins at around 160 degrees Celsius and produces progressively darker colour and deeper flavour up to around 180 degrees Celsius; beyond this point the sugar moves quickly toward a burnt, acrid taste.

content.text: Kouign-amann is a Breton butter cake. Butter and sugar are folded into a bread dough through rough
lamination
, then baked hard. The outside
caramelises
to a brittle golden crust.
The outer edges are flaky. The middle is tender and pull-apart. The base seals to a layer of crunchy, bittersweet caramel.
Watch the tin in the final 10 minutes. The caramel moves from deep amber to burnt in about 3 minutes. Keep your eye on it.
Ingredients

items.prepNote: divided: 100 g for folding into the dough, 50 g for the tin

content.text: Method
Making the dough and bulk ferment

Combine the flour, yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Keep salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl until you begin mixing, as direct contact can slow the yeast. Add the warm water and mix to a rough dough, then turn out onto an unfloured surface and knead for 5 minutes until smooth and slightly springy. The dough will be quite soft. Shape into a ball, return to the bowl, cover with a clean cloth or cling film, and leave at room temperature for 1 hour until roughly doubled in size.
Folding in butter and sugar

Lightly flour your work surface. Turn the risen dough out and roll it into a rectangle approximately 40 cm x 20 cm. Scatter the cold butter slabs over two-thirds of the rectangle. Sprinkle half the sugar (50 g) over the butter. Fold the unbuttered third over the centre, then fold the remaining third over the top (a letter fold). Press the edges lightly to seal. Chill for 20 minutes.

Repeat: roll the folded dough back out to 40 cm x 20 cm. Scatter the remaining 50 g of sugar across the surface. Fold again in the same way. If at any point the butter looks shiny and greasy, or the dough feels warm, stop and refrigerate for 20 minutes. If sugar crystals burst through the dough as you roll, do not try to push them back in; they will dissolve in the oven.
Shaping in the tin
Generously butter a 22 to 23 cm round cake tin. Scatter the 50 g of sugar reserved for the tin evenly across the base and sides.

Roll or press the dough into a rough round that fits the tin. It does not need to be perfect: ragged edges and irregular thickness are part of the character of this cake. Press the dough into the tin, pushing it gently into the edges. Some sugar will mix with any butter that has seeped out and form a slick on the base; this is correct.
Sprinkle a pinch of flaky sea salt over the top if using. Leave the cake to prove for 20 to 30 minutes at room temperature. It will puff slightly but this is not a dramatic rise.
Baking

Heat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius (conventional). Bake for 30 to 35 minutes. During the last 10 minutes the caramel will bubble vigorously at the edges and may produce a little smoke; this is normal. The cake is done when it is a deep amber brown across the entire surface and the edges are beginning to pull away from the sides of the tin.

This is the critical step: as soon as the cake comes out of the oven, leave it to cool in the tin for exactly 5 minutes. Any less and the caramel is dangerously hot liquid; any more and it sets solid and glues the cake to the tin. At 5 minutes, run a palette knife firmly around the edge, then invert the cake decisively onto a wire rack. The caramel base is now on top. Leave to cool for at least 15 minutes before cutting. The caramel will harden as it cools.

attrs.problem: The cake is stuck in the tin and will not invert
attrs.avoid: Avoid waiting more than 5 to 6 minutes before turning the cake out. The caramel sets solid as it cools and acts as a very effective glue.
attrs.fix: Return the tin to the oven for 2 to 3 minutes to re-melt the caramel, then invert immediately. Butter the tin extremely generously next time.

attrs.problem: The caramel tastes burnt rather than bittersweet
attrs.avoid: Avoid leaving the cake unattended during the final 10 minutes. The caramelisation window between deep amber and burnt is narrow.
attrs.fix: If the edges look very dark before the centre has caramelised, lay a sheet of foil loosely over the top of the tin. Next time, check the cake at 28 minutes and use a lighter-coloured tin if available.

attrs.problem: The butter leaked out onto the tray and the cake is greasy rather than layered
attrs.avoid: Avoid rolling with butter that has softened and become shiny or oily. Cold butter integrates as distinct layers; warm butter melts directly into the dough.
attrs.fix: Refrigerate the dough for 20 minutes between folds next time. If you see greasy smearing during rolling, stop immediately and chill before continuing.

attrs.problem: The dough barely rose during the bulk ferment
attrs.avoid: Avoid placing the bowl in a cold draught or near an air conditioning vent during the rise.
attrs.fix: Check that the water used for the dough was warm (35 degrees Celsius) and not hot (which kills yeast) or cold. If your kitchen is below 20 degrees Celsius, place the bowl inside the oven with just the oven light on, which raises the temperature slightly without applying heat.
